## One framework for all daily methods

For an idealised diurnal profile between \(T_{min}\) and \(T_{max}\), define

* the **excess** \(I(x) = \frac{1}{P}\int_0^P \max(0, T(t) - x)\,dt\), and
* the **exceedance** \(F(x)\), the fraction of the day with \(T(t) > x\).

Both depend only on the distribution of temperatures within the day. For a
sine wave with mean \(M\) and amplitude \(A\), with
\(\theta = \arcsin((x - M)/A)\),

\[
I(x) = \frac{1}{\pi}\left[(M - x)\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right) + A\cos\theta\right],
\qquad F(x) = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{\theta}{\pi},
\]

which is the Baskerville-Emin (1969) formula. For a symmetric triangle
\(I(x) = (T_{max} - x)^2 / (2(T_{max} - T_{min}))\) when
\(T_{min} < x < T_{max}\).

With a lower threshold \(L\) and an upper threshold \(U\):

| Cutoff | Degree-days | Development above \(U\) |
|---|---|---|
| none | \(I(L)\) | unbounded |
| horizontal | \(I(L) - I(U)\) | constant at \(U - L\) |
| vertical | \(I(L) - I(U) - (U - L)F(U)\) | zero |
| intermediate | \(I(L) - 2I(U) + I(2U - L)\) | decreases with slope -1 |

Double methods split the day into a rising half (\(T_{min,d} \to T_{max,d}\))
and a falling half (\(T_{max,d} \to T_{min,d+1}\)), each contributing half a
day.

## Methods compared

```{r}
tmin <- 8; tmax <- seq(10, 40, by = 1)
methods <- c("average", "modified_average", "single_sine", "single_triangle")
cols <- c("grey40", "#8E5BA8", "#0B5563", "#E8702A")
gdd <- sapply(methods, function(m) degree_days(rep(tmin, length(tmax)), tmax,
                                               method = m, base = 10))
matplot(tmax, gdd, type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2, col = cols,
        xlab = "Tmax (degC), Tmin = 8 degC", ylab = "GDD base 10 (degC day)")
legend("topleft", legend = methods, lty = 1, lwd = 2, bty = "n", col = cols)
```

When \(T_{min} < T_b < T_{max}\) the averaging method underestimates heat
accumulation because it ignores the warm hours (a consequence of Jensen's
inequality for the convex function \(\max(0, T - T_b)\)).

The **modified average** (McMaster & Wilhelm 1997, method 2) raises
\(T_{min}\) to \(T_b\) and caps \(T_{max}\) at \(T_u\) before averaging.
It counts part of the warm hours on cool days, but it is not an integral of
the diurnal profile: with \(T_{min} < T_b\) it lies above the averaging
method and, in this example, also above the sine and triangle methods,
because replacing \(T_{min}\) by \(T_b\) assigns the base temperature to
the whole cool part of the day. It is the standard method for maize in the
United States (\(T_b = 10\), \(T_u = 30\) degrees C, the "86/50" rule).

## Cutoffs are not interchangeable

```{r}
tmax <- seq(20, 45, by = 1)
cuts <- c("horizontal", "intermediate", "vertical")
gdd <- sapply(cuts, function(k) degree_days(rep(15, length(tmax)), tmax,
                                            base = 10, upper = 30, cutoff = k))
matplot(tmax, gdd, type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2,
        col = c("#0B5563", "#5DA9C9", "#E8702A"),
        xlab = "Tmax (degC), Tmin = 15 degC",
        ylab = "GDD (degC day), base 10, upper 30")
legend("topleft", legend = cuts, lty = 1, lwd = 2, bty = "n",
       col = c("#0B5563", "#5DA9C9", "#E8702A"))
```

## Hourly data

With hourly observations use `degree_hours()`; the conversion to degree-days
divides the daily sum by 24:

```{r}
temp <- 12 + 9 * sin(2 * pi * (0:47 - 9) / 24)
degree_hours(temp, base = 10, by_day = TRUE)
```

## Which method?

The differences above are exact consequences of each formula. How large
they are in practice depends on the climate and on the data available
(hourly, daily or monthly). The article
[Degree-day methods compared on synthetic temperatures](https://djwillichile.github.io/thermify/articles/gdd-synthetic.html)
quantifies them with synthetic hourly series for four sites in the Maule
Region. With daily extremes, the triangle methods and the hourly
reconstruction stayed within about 1 % of the hourly integral, the sine
methods overestimated by about 2 %, the averaging method underestimated by
2-6 % and the modified average overestimated by 7-11 % (base 10 degrees C,
heat season). These results are synthetic and must be confirmed with
observed hourly records (`vignette("validation")`).

## Ensembles

No single method is best everywhere, so thermify can combine them.
`gdd_ensemble_weights()` estimates the weights from `validate_station()`
results, that is, from **observed** hourly records, with three schemes:

* `"stacking"` (default): the non-negative weights that sum to one and
  minimise the squared error. Methods with opposite biases, such as the
  averaging (too low) and the sine (too high) methods, can be combined.
* `"bma"`: Bayesian model averaging; weights follow each method's
  likelihood.
* `"akaike"`: Akaike weights, \(w_k \propto \exp(-\Delta AIC_k / 2)\).
  The methods have no fitted parameters, so the AIC penalty is the same for
  all of them and the weights are relative likelihoods: with many seasons
  they tend to select one method rather than combine several.

BMA and Akaike weights reward the single best method; stacking rewards the
best combination. The fitted object reports cross-validated errors (leaving
one station out); use the ensemble only when it beats the best single
method in cross-validation.

thermify ships no default weights. The weights below are illustrative only:

```{r}
w <- c(average = 0.4, single_sine = 0.6)   # illustrative, not estimated
gdd_ensemble(c(4, 8, 12), c(18, 24, 31), weights = w, base = 10)
```

`gdd_ensemble()` returns the members and their spread (`sd`, `min`, `max`)
as a measure of method uncertainty. With estimated weights, use
`degree_days(method = "ensemble", weights = w)` or
`thermify(..., gdd_methods = "ensemble", gdd_weights = w)`.

## References

Baskerville & Emin (1969); Lindsey & Newman (1956); Sevacherian et al.
(1977); Allen (1976); Zalom et al. (1983); McMaster & Wilhelm (1997). Full
citations are in `?degree_days`.
